 Casper Ruud is one of the names of the week at the ATP Paris , where he is already in the quarterfinals after defeating Jan-Lennard Struff yesterday. Once he sealed his victory, the Norwegian player shared a harsh reflection on modern tennis and why there are fewer epic matches , and also analyzed the challenge for him to change his style in order to remain at the top of the rankings. 
 Ruud visited the 'Tennis Channel' table last night, where he talked about the match and how his game has evolved in response to the needs of the tour . Casper's heavy topspin allowed him to become world number 2 at one point, reach several Grand Slam finals, and come just one win away from being world number 1 , but all that has changed. "The most challenging part of changing my game has been that most players play at a high pace from both sides these days, and I prefer to work through points and play with topspin , a bit like we saw Nadal and Thiem do. They were my idols growing up, and I think I have had to accept that players are able to defend the topspin shot a bit better ," he stated.
 In fact, the Norwegian player opened up about modern tennis, stating that " there won't be as many great matches in this modern tennis, because everyone serves well, returns well, and attacks whenever they see an opening. I haven't always had the audacity to go for the big shots only when I see a real opportunity. I've been a bit passive because my game was more about working the opponent gradually , maybe looking for the error, or until I got an even easier shot, but you see other players and they hit the ball in any way these days, and I try to do that a bit more with my tennis, but it's still a continuous challenge, and probably will be for the rest of my career ."
 The key to Ruud's victory over Struff 
 Throughout the week, Ruud has been playing very aggressively and not allowing his opponents to breathe , as seen against Rafa Jódar or just yesterday against Struff. It’s curious that a player whose game adapts more to clay courts is thriving on the fastest surface of the season, but his forehand is running a lot and with his backhand he is varying heights to confuse his opponents. Additionally, Casper believes that his return has played a key role in his results.
 "The short return is working well on this fast court, and I think much of this has to do with good footwork and trying to be quick. With Struff, you have to be careful with his serve and volley , obviously, but when I broke him in the first set I made a couple of good returns and that was key. I have struggled in the past playing against someone who serves and volleys because I've been too far back and my returns have been too high and floating, and they come in and put the volley away, but today I was reading his serve very well and I think that made him stay a bit further back in the second and I took advantage of that," he concluded.
 In tennis, you either reinvent yourself or you stagnate, and Ruud has chosen the first option. To return to the top spots in the rankings, Casper knows he must be more aggressive, step up, and play within the court during rallies. Moreover, he has the qualities to do so, especially with his forehand. Therefore, this tournament may be a turning point for the Norwegian player to find the path to redemption after a season with more shadows than lights.
